summary:
Gangwon province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, and gender identity and gender expression are not offences in civilian life. The criminalising provision that survives, Military Criminal Act article 92-6, reaches consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023.

Restroom access is governed by a national standard that reaches Gangwon directly. In July 2024 a Seoul appellate court finalised a 300,000 won damages award against the state, holding that police advice telling a person who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom forms part of the same standard. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to do so, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether.

Legal gender recognition without surgery is the operative rule in the province. In May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved registered-sex change from male to female for five applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria and that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity.

No Gangwon-specific ordinance, police practice, incident or enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors is documented in these sources, so the rules a visitor meets in the province are the national ones described above.
tangentialFactors:
The restroom litigation and the Yeongdong surgical-prerequisite ruling both arose in other provinces but bind Gangwon as national standards; a trans visitor to Gangwon can rely on them, though no local case has yet tested them there.

National survey data on restroom avoidance and discrimination burden indicates that everyday facilities access remains a practical difficulty for trans people regardless of the favourable rulings, since the rulings establish liability rather than change on-the-ground conditions.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Gangwon who change their registered sex can do so without sex-reassignment surgery under the Yeongdong court's reasoning, which treats prior surgical guidelines as reference only.

Residents denied restroom access, or given police advice to avoid gender-appropriate restrooms, have a documented basis for damages claims against the state or the excluding institution, following the Seoul appellate and Daegu District Court awards.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Gangwon-specific incident, ordinance, police practice or court case involving trans people appears in the source inventory; the province-level picture is unresolved beyond the national standards that apply.

Whether Gangwon provincial police or schools have issued restroom or facilities guidance consistent with the 2024 appellate ruling is not sourced here.
